findings.breaking_input: privateRoot = join(ARC_PRIVATE_DIR || homedir(), "launch", a.venture) where a.venture is "../repo" (a venture slug a user can pass). The loop starts at resolve(privateRoot) — ~/.arc-private/launch/../repo — checks it is not a link and that no ancestor holds .git, but ~/.arc-private/launch/../repo/... resolves into the venture repo itself; .git is found at the repo root and refused. But a.venture = "a/b" with ARC_PRIVATE_DIR = "/tmp/x" where /tmp/x/launch/a/b/thing.git exists (a git dir far away): the loop walks up to /tmp/x/launch/a where .git does not exist, walks further. The real break: the loop checks `.git` existence but only after resolve; if ARC_PRIVATE_DIR is a path containing a component that is a symlink to a dir (e.g., ARC_PRIVATE_DIR = /home/user/private-link where private-link -> /var/tmp/evil), the loop resolves the symlink at mkdir time — resolve() does not resolve symlinks, so lstatSync(d) for the symlink component itself is never checked because the loop checks each d after resolve, and resolve() returns the lexical path with the symlink as a normal component. writeFileSync then follows the symlinked privateRoot, writing the SUPABASE_DB_URL into /var/tmp/evil. Nothing ever lstat-checked the privateRoot components.
findings.why: The code comment says "every existing ancestor, lexical and real, is asked for a .git, and any existing ancestor that is a link refuses", but the loop only lstat's the resolved path d; a symlink in ARC_PRIVATE_DIR's own components is not checked because resolve() does not resolve them and the loop starts at the full resolved privateRoot, so the symlink component is an ancestor that is skipped. This is the twin of the prior `ctx.write` ancestor-link fix: the fix checked only leaf and only lexical resolve.
findings.fix: After mkdir, call realpathSync(privateRoot) and verify every component of the real path (from the filesystem root) is not a symlink, or refuse ARC_PRIVATE_DIR if any component is a link. Also write with O_NOFOLLOW.
findings.twin_of: `ctx.write` resolved symlinks only on the ancestors, so a LEAF link carried a write out of the venture root

findings.breaking_input: privateRoot = "/repo/.git/../launch/fx" or any path whose lexical resolution contains ".git" as a traversed component but where realpathSync(d) normalizes it away. The check asks `existsSync(join(d, ".git")) || existsSync(join(realpathSync(d), ".git"))`. If the path is `/repo/.git/../launch/fx`, the lexical join(d, ".git") is `/repo/.git/../launch/fx/.git` (does not exist), and realpathSync(d) resolves to `/repo/launch/fx` so realpathSync(d)/.git is also absent. The write lands inside a path that the terminal caller sees as inside the .git dir, so a credential can be written inside a repo's .git internals (or inside a work tree when the lexical path passes through .git). Conversely, if a work tree is reached only through a symlinked component that resolves into another tree, realpathSync may follow it and find .git, but the lexical component check is on a path that has already been traversed.
findings.why: The check validates the real path and the lexical path separately, but a path that traverses `.git` as a lexical intermediate (e.g. `/repo/.git/../launch`) evades both: the lexical join to .git looks at `/repo/.git/../launch/.git` and the real path collapses the `.git` segment. This is a 'validate one read, use another' defect on the private-dir boundary.
findings.fix: Refuse any component of the resolve()d path that equals `.git` before the final dirname loop, or after realpath, compare the real path's components to the lexical path's components for a `.git` anywhere in the traversed prefix.
findings.twin_of: The git-tree check read the lexical path

findings.breaking_input: A worker that exits 4 with `after.state === 'pending'` and `after.reason` starting exactly with `PENDING(` is classed as pending. The worker writes the state file, then the runner reads it. If an adapter (or any other writer to the state JSON) writes `state: "pending"` with `reason: "PENDING(..."` for a different cause — e.g. a fixture that reuses the pending state for a genuinely failed slot, or a bug where a failed reason is prefixed by PENDING( — the runner returns EXIT.DEPS (exit 4) and stops the walk instead of failing. More concretely, the fake provider's `FAKE_PENDING` can be set to an empty string: `if FAKE_PENDING=""` then `pending` is the empty string, and `pendingWhy` in verify mode becomes `PENDING()` because the check is `typeof v.pending === 'string'` (empty passes), so it constructs `PENDING()`, and the outcome check `String(after.reason).startsWith("PENDING(")` passes for `PENDING()`. An empty reason is then treated as waiting, and the slot stays pending forever on an empty string even though nothing is actually pending.
findings.why: The runner keys the outcome 'pending' on a free-text reason prefix and the state field, with no requirement that the pending string is non-empty or that the exit code 4 was actually produced by the new PENDING path (any exit 4 with pending state and a PENDING( reason qualifies). An adapter or fixture that answers `{ok:false, pending:""}` (empty pending) is mis-read as waiting. This is a 'decision reads free text' defect.
findings.fix: In the worker, require `v.pending` to be non-empty (`typeof v.pending === 'string' && v.pending.trim() !== ''`), and in the runner require `after.reason` to be `PENDING(` with a non-empty payload. Better: pass the outcome through a structured field rather than a reason prefix.
findings.twin_of: --again keyed on the gate string only

findings.breaking_input: A production deployment `d` with `created` as an ISO string (Vercel returns `created` as an integer but a malicious or older record can return `"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"`). `Number(d.created)` -> NaN, `later(at)` filters `Number(d.created) > at` which is `NaN > at` = false, so a genuinely newer READY deployment is never considered; `ours` READY returns null (ok), so a READY build of the wrong (older) commit passes because `ours` is READY. Conversely, if `ours` is BUILDING and a newer READY build exists but its `created` is ISO, `newerReady` returns false and the slot answers pending forever, wedging the walk. Also, the `descends` compare uses `gh(..., [404])` and checks `r.status === 200`; but `gh` may return a 200 with a body lacking `status` (e.g. the compare API returns `status:"diverged"` for unrelated branches, handled, but a 200 with `status:"unknown"` is read as false, and a 200 with no body -> false). A 200 with `status:"behind"` (sha is ahead of the newer commit, i.e. the newer commit is an ancestor) is read as false, so a legitimate rollback that IS the headers' content (a newer commit that descends) is rejected — but more critical: a 200 with `status:"ahead"` is accepted even when the newer commit is on an unrelated fork that happens to be ahead of sha, because `compare` only asks 'is the newer commit ahead of sha' without checking it descends from the same branch. A hotfix branch with a commit that is not a descendant of sha but has a commit SHA greater in the compare's graph could be 'ahead' if it shares an ancestor but diverges, and `status:"ahead"` is only set when the other commit has no unique commits against the base — compare returns "ahead" when the base has no commits after the other; with a diverged history it returns "diverged". So a truly diverged build is not accepted, but a build with an ancestor relationship on a different lineage (e.g. a cherry-pick that GitHub compares as "ahead") is accepted as proof the headers shipped.
findings.why: `newerReady` confirms ancestry via GitHub compare but trusts the first `later()` entry that returns status ahead/identical without checking the commit's branch or that the deployment's commit is actually a descendant (compare 'ahead' can be true for a commit that is an ancestor of sha, i.e. the headers commit is a descendant of the newer commit, meaning the newer build does NOT carry the headers). The compare `sha...c` returns 'ahead' when c is ahead of sha, but 'ahead' does not mean c descends from sha — it means c has no commits that sha lacks? Actually GitHub compare 'ahead' means the other branch has no commits not in the base; with a divergent history it returns 'diverged'. The code accepts 'ahead' or 'identical' — but a newer commit can be 'ahead' when it is a different lineage that shares no unique commits against sha, e.g. a squashed commit of the same content on a separate branch whose ancestry is unrelated. So the new build may not actually be the same toolchain. The deeper point: the acceptance of ANY READY build whose commit compares ahead or identical, on a single page, is the twin of 'verify found some green run, not launch's'.
findings.fix: Require the newer deployment's commit to be an ancestor of sha (i.e. compare returns 'behind' or 'identical' meaning sha is ahead or equal), or fetch the deployment's branch/PR and match it to the headers config branch. Never count a newer build from a different branch as proof.
findings.twin_of: A verify took the newest green run without asking which commit it ran on

findings.breaking_input: The worker's PENDING block checks `v.ok === false && typeof v.pending === 'string' && v.pending && typeof v.answerer === 'string' && v.answerer`. If the adapter returns `v.pending` as a string containing only whitespace (`" "`), the truthiness check passes (non-empty) and `cut(v.pending, 160)` produces `PENDING(   )` after `clean`. The runner's `PENDING(` prefix matches, so a whitespace reason counts as pending. More importantly, `v.pending` can contain control characters and newlines; `cut` applies `clean` which drops C0/C1 but not other content, and `PENDING(` is built by `[...clean(v.pending)].slice(0,160).join("")` — a pending string with a newline from the adapter (e.g. an adapter misreads a deployment description with `\n`) becomes `PENDING(what\n...)`, and the runner's stop line `clean(fin.reason)` may reformat but the state reason already has a newline, which can forge a board line. The runner's own test asserts `reason` is exactly `PENDING(build: deployment dpl_x is BUILDING)`, but a pending string with a trailing line break and a fake "stopped at" text can inject a line into the board output.
findings.why: The PENDING reason is clean()ed for display but the stored state reason is built from adapter-controlled text with only `clean` (C0/C1 and bidi marks removed), and the runner treats the prefix as the authoritative signal. A newline in the adapter's pending text reaches the state file and the board output — the twin of 'adapter-supplied strings printed raw'.
findings.fix: Build the stored reason with the full `say`/single-line sanitisation (replace line breaks with spaces) before wrapping in PENDING(), and require `pending` to be non-empty after trimming.
findings.twin_of: Adapter-supplied strings (resource ids, reasons, answerers) were printed raw

findings.where: next-headers.mjs buildGate: `ds.find(d => d.meta && d.meta.githubCommitSha === sha)` and `later`/`newerReady` with `Number(ours.created)`
findings.breaking_input: The deployments page returns `d.created` as a string "" (empty), or the deployment object has `created: 0`. `Number("0") = 0`; `later(0)` accepts any newer READY deployment with `created > 0`. A deployment with `created: 0` (or mis-parsed ISO) for `ours` makes every other deployment count as newer, so a READY preview or a build of an unrelated commit that happens to be in the same page is accepted as proof the headers shipped, even if the unrelated commit descends from sha (compare 'ahead' on a divergent branch). The `later` filter takes the first 3 READY deployments with a valid 40-hex commit sha, but does not check their `target` is production; the API query sets target=production but a provider or a manipulated response can include preview deployments. The proxy fixture sets `target: 'production'` on all, but the real Vercel API can return deployments with `target: null` (the older Vercel field is `projectId` and `target` may be absent for legacy). A READY deployment with no `target` field passes `later` and `descends`, and if it is newer it counts as proof the headers are live, though it may be a preview.
findings.why: `later` only requires a valid sha, not that the deployment is production or that the sha descends from the headers commit's branch in a strict sense (compare 'ahead' is not ancestry). Combined with `Number(ours.created)` where `ours.created` could be an ISO string, a preview or unrelated build can satisfy newerReady. This is the twin of 'verify matched the preview by branch sha without asking whose branch it was'.
findings.fix: In the deployments filter, require `d.target === 'production'` and `d.meta.githubCommitSha` to be present; and make `descends` require the newer commit to be a strict descendant by comparing the compare API's `ahead_by`/`behind_by` fields, refusing 'ahead' unless it means the newer commit is strictly ahead with no divergence.
findings.twin_of: verify matched the preview by branch sha without asking whose branch it was

findings.breaking_input: A malicious or misconfigured RDAP server (or a MITM of the pinned DoH? no, RDAP not pinned) answers `{ ldhName: "evil.com", ... }` for a query to `/domain/myfitfolio.com`. The adapter never checks that `json.ldhName` equals the queried domain. `verify` returns ok:true with evidence for `myfitfolio.com` when the record actually describes `evil.com` — a different domain satisfies the 'registered, not expiring' test, and the evidence carries the wrong name. The fixture sets `ldhName: NAME.toUpperCase()` but the real RDAP could return a different name (or an `ldhName` with a trailing dot or a Unicode variant). Also a domain with an upper-case TLD like `myfitfolio.COM` — `d` is lowercased by `bare`, but RDAP `ldhName` may be `myfitfolio.COM`; `.toLowerCase()` in the check would normalize, but there is no check.
findings.why: The adapter must prove it read the record for the domain it asked about; otherwise a stale or malicious record from the registry host (which is in the row's hosts[]) can make an unregistered or held domain appear registered. This is the twin of 'A verify proved some file at that path, not launch's file'.
findings.fix: In `rdapFacts` or verify, require `bare(json && json.ldhName) === d`; otherwise return `{ ok:false, reason: "rdap:name-mismatch" }`.
findings.twin_of: A verify proved "some file at that path" and "some green run", not launch's file under that run

findings.breaking_input: An existing `launch_backup` role with comment exactly equal to `ctx.tag` is accepted as launch's and skipped; the adapter returns `note: "exists (launch's); its URL was written when it was made"` without writing a private file. If the role actually exists but the owner lost the URL, or a previous run created the role and the private-file write was never performed (e.g. the earlier fix B1 called for rotating the password but the current code does NOT rotate — the code only re-writes the file on the create path, not on the exists path), then the owner is told the URL was written when it was made, but there is no URL on disk. The breaking input: a role with the tag exists and the private file `SUPABASE_DB_URL` does not exist (e.g. the file was deleted, or the earlier write failed after the role was created despite the intended write-before-create order). The adapter returns success; the owner has no credential and the slot is marked verified.
findings.why: The exists path trusts the role comment and returns a note that the URL was written, but never checks whether the file actually exists or rewrites it. The half-made state 'role exists, file missing' is read as complete. This is the twin of 'An absent hold was re-placed, re-holding a live venture after release deleted the file' and the B1 fix for the two-step create, which redesigned the order but did not make the exists path self-healing.
findings.fix: On the exists path, check `existsSync(join(privateRoot, 'SUPABASE_DB_URL'))`; if missing, rotate the password with an `alter role` (inside the same transaction as the rewrite) and write the file, or refuse with a clear 'URL missing; rerun after teardown' error.
findings.twin_of: launch's own credential was never refreshed

findings.where: vercel-env-store.mjs place (report-then-create but kill between POST and report is now report-before-create, fixed) — but the POST failure still reports the resource first
findings.breaking_input: The code reports the resource (`ctx.report(r)`) BEFORE the POST. If the POST fails, the resource `vercel-env prj:KEY` is recorded as launch's, and teardown will later delete a key that launch never placed (the owner's? Actually the key was not set, so teardown deleting a non-existent key is harmless). The real break: if the POST times out (transport) and the request actually succeeded on Vercel (a network partition), the code throws with no response, the resource is already reported, so re-run sees the key in `set` and skips — fine. But if the POST fails with a non-ok status (e.g. 400 rate limit) AFTER the value was actually written? No write on failure. The concrete issue: report-before-create records intent, but if the run is killed after the report is persisted but before the POST is even sent (e.g. the worker dies on the next line), a resource is recorded as launch's when nothing was placed, and teardown will delete a future owner-set key that now exists because teardown deletes by name regardless of who set it since. The ownership model 'production lacks it now' means a later owner setting that key (after this failed run) will be deleted by teardown as launch's, because the resource was recorded without a create ever happening.
findings.why: Report-before-create is the intended fix for B6, but a kill between report and POST leaves a resource record that claims a create that never happened; the resource id is the key name, and teardown deletes by recorded id. A later owner key of the same name is then deleted as launch's. The older defect 'A resource was reported only after a later call succeeded' is replaced by 'reported even when the create never ran'.
findings.fix: Record the intent with a marker (e.g. report only after the POST resolves, but also persist a 'pending' record that is cleared on failure; or record with an extra field 'created_at' and make teardown confirm the key exists and its type/value matches a recorded fingerprint before deleting).
findings.twin_of: A resource was reported only after a later call succeeded, so a failure in between left an unrecorded commit -> the inverse: reported without ever creating

findings.breaking_input: The two resolvers must agree with Cloudflare's assigned nameservers. The DoH responses are parsed by `nsOf`, which takes `a.data` where `a.data` could be `null` or `[object Object]`. `bare(say(a.data, 253))` on a null becomes `""`. If a resolver returns an NS answer whose `data` field is a number (0) — `String(0)` = "0" — the mapped list contains "0". The assigned list from Cloudflare is nameservers like `meera.ns.cloudflare.com`. `sameSet` will be false and the check fails (safe). But if the resolver returns `data` as a string that is a non-ASCII lookalike (e.g. a full-width dot) that sorts and compares equal? No. The real bypass: the check only compares the SET of names, not that the names belong to the domain's parent (Cloudflare could assign `meera.ns.cloudflare.com` and the resolver could return that same set even though the domain is actually delegated elsewhere — the resolver is controlled by the provider? The resolvers are pinned by ctx.probe and are honest by assumption). A more concrete logic gap: `sameSet` uses `a.every((x) => b.includes(x))` after both are sorted; but the Cloudflare `zone.name_servers` field can include values with a trailing dot or uppercase; `bare` handles trailing dot and lowercase. The defect: if Cloudflare reports `name_servers` with a leading dot (`".meera.ns.cloudflare.com"`), `bare` does not strip a leading dot, so the check fails (false negative, not a bypass). Energy: the real miss is that the code never checks the delegation is the APEX; `nsOf` takes the resolver answer for the apex, and the resolver could be answering a cached old NS set while the live delegation changed; that is an inherent third-party trust, not logic.
findings.why: No clean bypass; the logic does check the sets strictly. Not a real finding; report only if there is a concrete mismatch like nameserver count > 13 being truncated: `slice(0,13)` truncates a resolver answer with 14 NS records — Cloudflare assigns at most 2, so truncated is fine. Drop this.

findings.where: worker.mjs PENDING in verify mode (last_verify overwrite)
findings.breaking_input: When `verify` mode gets a pending answer, `last_verify` is overwritten to `{ ok: false, reason: "PENDING(...)" }` and the worker exits 1. The runner's verify command (not the apply command) reads the worker exit status: the new runner code only added exit-4 handling for the apply path (status===4 && state pending), not for verify mode where the worker exits 1. The runner's verify mode paths likely treat exit 1 as a failed verify. The test `launch-runner: verify of a pending build names PENDING in its answer and never changes the slot` only asserts the state file's slot row stays `verified` and that `last_verify.reason` is PENDING; it does not assert the runner's verify command exit status. The `verify --all` command (which reads last_verify or the worker exit) will report failure. This was already D49 in the debt ledger, but the reported finding L15 is fixed only by an assertion that the slot row stays verified; the runner's `verify` mode still treats a pending worker exit 1 as a failure, so `apply --all` after a `verify` that hit a pending may stop at that slot as failed if the runner consults last_verify in the walk. The existing fix is incomplete.
findings.why: The code comment and the new runner branch only cover the apply mode (worker exit 4). The verify mode still saves a non-ok last_verify and exits 1, and nothing in the runner's verify path translates that to 'pending'. This is exactly the debt D49, which is listed as kept, not fixed.
findings.fix: In verify mode, when the answer is pending, keep the previous last_verify.ok (or add a `pending: true` field), and change the runner to treat a worker exit 1 with last_verify.reason starting PENDING( as a non-fatal pending (exit 4) in verify --all too.
findings.twin_of: A saved ok was trusted after any exit
